name: Floodplain forest
notes: Riparian bottomland forest of fast-growing cottonwoods, willows, sycamore and silver maple that tolerate seasonal flooding, over cane, dogwood and tall nettle/fern ground cover threaded with vines; drawn on the Mississippi/Missouri bottoms and the Rhine/Danube floodplains.

canopy.name: Bald cypress

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: 3-9 (usually 6) cotyledons, then soft, flat, feathery needles in two ranks on deciduous side shoots; seedlings grow 20-75 cm in their first year if not flooded over. The sapling is a slender, pyramidal cone; buttress and knees come later and the crown flattens with age. Foliage turns copper-red and drops in autumn.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of N. America (seedlings 20-75 cm in year 1; soil saturated but not flooded 1-3 months for germination; intermediate shade tolerance; height growth stops ~200 yr); Wikipedia (3 m at 5 yr, 21 m at 41 yr, 36 m at 96 yr; seed from ~30 yr; 3-9 cotyledons; Black River tree at least 2,624 yr old).

growth.juvenile_note: Cottony seed germinates within 24-48 h on wet, bare sandbars and mud flats; the seedling has two minute cotyledons and grows slowly for about 3 weeks, then very fast. Dense, even-aged thickets of slender single-stemmed whips form along river bars, with large triangular, coarsely toothed leaves on flattened stalks that flutter; saplings add 1.5-3.5 m a year on good sites.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (P. deltoides: germination within 48 h; slow first 3 weeks then very rapid; seed from 5-10 yr, plains ~10 yr; 1.8-3.7 m/yr; very intolerant of shade; short-lived, 80-90 yr); USDA FEIS (eastern 100-200 yr, plains ~90 yr; 3-58 m tall).

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics vol. 2 (flowers Feb-Apr east, Apr-May plains, before leaves; male catkins 8-13 cm, female 15-30 cm; 3-4-valved capsules with 30-60 seeds ripen in 30-60 days; up to 48 million seeds per tree; wind pollinated); FEIS (capsules 0.8-1.5 cm). Colour is the red male catkins.

canopy.name: Southern magnolia

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two fleshy oblong cotyledons, then glossy evergreen leaves, smaller and thinner than the adult's and less rusty-felted beneath. The sapling is a dense, pyramidal evergreen with a single straight leader and branches down to the ground (46-61 cm in its first year in a nursery). It endures shade for years; flowers start at about 10 years.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (Magnolia grandiflora: seed from age 10, optimum ~25; nursery seedlings 46-61 cm in year 1; 18-24 m at 80-120 yr; tolerant of shade when young); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (epigeal, germination in 30-50 days after stratification)

canopy.name: Green ash

growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (Kennedy, green ash): seed-bearing from about age 20, good crops most years; samaras dispersed autumn to spring; epigeal; moderately tolerant of shade; to 120 yr or more; first-bottom tree with cottonwood, black willow and silver maple

ground.name: Ostrich fern

growth.juvenile_note: Green, short-lived spores germinate within days into heart-shaped gametophytes; the sporeling's first fronds are tiny and simple, then small pinnate fronds unroll from a little crown. It builds a stout upright crown that each spring unrolls a shuttlecock (vase) of feathery sterile fronds, with stiff brown fertile fronds in the middle from autumn; underground stolons start new crowns nearby.
growth.source: Wikipedia Matteuccia (sterile fronds 100-170 cm, fertile fronds 40-65 cm develop in autumn, persist over winter and shed spores in early spring; lateral stolons form new crowns and dense colonies on riverbanks); fern sporeling timings and ages estimated

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.name: River oats

growth.juvenile_note: Seed washed onto banks by floods comes up in spring as a tuft of broad, bamboo-like flat leaves; it widens by short rhizomes into a clump and flowers in its second summer, the flat spikelets dangling on thread-like stalks.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 25 (Chasmanthium latifolium: perennial, shortly rhizomatous, 60-150 cm, flowers June-September); USDA Plants

repro.note: flat spikelets shatter in autumn and ride floodwater along the banks

ground.source: Chasmanthium latifolium, river oats or inland sea-oats (Poaceae), Kew POWO accepted; Pennsylvania and Michigan to Florida, west to Kansas and Texas, on alluvial banks and in floodplain and bottomland forest of the Mississippi and Missouri; 0.6-1.5 m — Flora of North America vol. 25; USDA Plants.

ground.name: Tree apron moss

growth.juvenile_note: Rarely produces capsules; new colonies mostly start from broken fragments that lodge on bark. Creeping stems send up short branches tapering to whip-like tips, and the colony slowly spreads into a dark green apron round the base of a trunk.
growth.source: Crum & Anderson, Mosses of Eastern North America (1981): Anomodon attenuatus, on tree bases, logs and shaded rock, sporophytes uncommon

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Anomodon attenuatus, tree apron moss (Anomodontaceae), accepted; eastern North America, Europe and Asia, in broad mats on the bases of hardwood trunks (elm, ash, maple), logs and shaded rock in floodplain and mesic forest; mats 1-4 cm deep — Crum & Anderson 1981; Flora of North America vol. 28.

leaf.notes: dull dark green to yellowish mats; creeping stems with ascending branches tapering to whip-like tips; brownish and pressed flat when dry

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the mushroom is a days-long fruiting body. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through connected dead wood or litter; 'wind' = spores.

epiphyte.name: Spanish moss

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are minute grey tufts of thread-like leaves on bark, but most new plants start as windblown or bird-carried fragments. A young plant is a short, curly chain of silvery-grey scaly stems with 2-6 cm thread leaves, lengthening over years into festoons that hang 1-6 m (rarely 8 m) from branches, with tiny three-petalled flowers in spring.
growth.source: Wikipedia Spanish moss (leaves 2-6 cm x 1 mm; hanging festoons to 6 m, rarely 8 m; spreads by seed and by fragments carried by wind and nesting birds; small flowers with spreading petals). Seed germination, strand growth rate, first flowering and festoon age estimated.

repro.note: most bloom once then die, leaving pups; hummingbird-pollinated; tank species hold rainwater that frogs and insects breed in

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two oval, short-stalked cotyledons, then alternate, heart-shaped, coarsely toothed leaves on a thin green stem. In its first year the seedling is a short floppy shoot; forked tendrils opposite the leaves appear within a few nodes and it becomes a scrambling vine that sprawls over the ground or brush until it finds a stem to climb, then runs several metres a year toward light.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Vitis riparia): long-lived climbing vine with trunks several inches thick, hardy to -57 C; USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Vitis): riverbank grape seed needs about 90 days of cold stratification. Germination after stratification, growth, first fruiting and ages estimated from wild grapes.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (Vitis riparia): small fragrant white or greenish flowers Apr-Jun in loose panicles 4-15 cm, functionally dioecious; blue-black, sour, herbaceous, juicy berries 6-15 mm ripe in Aug-Sep, used for jelly, jam and wine. Pollinator mix, fruit set, persistence into winter and crop estimated.
